title: The Surprise in Terror

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A close portrait of a man with wide-open eyes and a startled, dramatic expression, shown in the style of late eighteenth-century French portraiture.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, medium, public-domain statement; date c. 1790 taken from the image file name because the page text is truncated; collection not stated)

context: An oil painting on canvas by the French artist Joseph Ducreux, dated about 1790 (the page text is cut off, so the year is taken from the image file name). The page tags it as a self-portrait and does not state the collection.

descriptions.k: Look at this face. His eyes are wide open and his mouth looks surprised. What do you think just happened? Show us the same face!
descriptions.g12: Joseph Ducreux painted a face full of surprise. The eyes are wide and the face is big in the picture. You can try making the same face. What do you think surprised him?
descriptions.g35: Joseph Ducreux painted The Surprise in Terror around 1790. The page tags it as a self-portrait, so the artist may have studied his own expression. The wide eyes and open face show a strong feeling. Why might a painter want to practice painting such an expression?
descriptions.g68: The Surprise in Terror (c. 1790) by Joseph Ducreux is an oil portrait tagged on its source page as a self-portrait. It puts a dramatic facial expression at the center, which was unusual for formal portraits of the time. How do eyes, mouth and pose communicate the feeling, and why might a painter choose to study such a moment?
descriptions.g910: Joseph Ducreux's The Surprise in Terror (c. 1790) turns the portrait toward exaggerated emotion rather than dignified calm. Tagged on its page as a self-portrait, it may be read as an experiment in expression. How do the face and the tight framing build intensity, and what do you think the painting asks of the viewer?
descriptions.g1112: The Surprise in Terror (c. 1790) shows Joseph Ducreux using portraiture as a study of expression, an interest tied to eighteenth-century curiosity about how emotions show on the face. Tagged as a self-portrait, it blurs the line between likeness and performance. How might the work be read as comedy, drama or scientific observation, and what evidence limits each reading?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium (oil on canvas) and page tag (Self-portraits) read from the arthistoryproject.com page text; the page text is cut off after 'c.' so the date c. 1790 comes from the image file name (1790) and is marked as approximate; the page labels the movement Baroque, which does not fit a French work of about 1790, so the accepted label Rococo is used. The collection is not stated. SENSITIVE: the sitter has a wide-eyed, startled expression. K-2 questions are kept playful (surprise, funny faces) and avoid the word scary; older bands discuss expression as an artistic study. Only page text was read; the image file was not visually inspected, and a person must view it to confirm it is suitable for all ages before release.

teacherNote.context: An oil portrait by the French artist Joseph Ducreux, dated about 1790; the source page tags it as a self-portrait and does not state the collection or give a complete date. The face shows a strong expression of surprise.
directions: Have students use hand mirrors to study a 'surprise' face and draw only the eyes, brows and mouth, then compare how lines change feeling.
Ask students to caption the painting in three different ways and discuss how each caption changes the mood.
Discuss why artists study facial expressions and how portraits can show feelings, not just appearance.
